prompt: By default, what does `page.goto()` wait for before it returns?

choices.text: Every request the page will make, including the ones its scripts send
choices.why: Requests a script makes after the page is ready are not part of what `goto` waits for; that is the whole gap this lesson is about.

choices.text: The browser's `load` event
choices.why: Right. The document and the files it names have arrived; data a script fetches afterwards may not have.

choices.text: The first element with text to be drawn
choices.why: `goto` does not look at the content at all; it waits for a browser event.

choices.text: A fixed half second after the address answers
choices.why: There is no fixed delay in `goto`; it waits for an event, however long that takes.

prompt: `at-load.mjs` holds the products back for 500 ms, and `goto` returns to a list with 0 products. What changed in the page?

choices.text: The script now runs before the HTML has arrived
choices.why: The order of document and script is the same in both runs; only the answer for products is later.

choices.text: The `load` event no longer fires
choices.why: It fires in both runs, and in the second it fires long before the products arrive.

choices.text: Nothing; only one answer arrived later
choices.why: Right. The page is the same, the race between `load` and the products had a different winner.

choices.text: The list was cleared by the routing
choices.why: The routing only delays the answer; the list was empty because nothing had filled it yet.

prompt: A page that asks the server for data without leaving the page, and without the browser waiting for that answer before calling the page ready, is loading it ___ .
The search route waits `max(0, 900 - 150 * length)` milliseconds. How long does it wait before answering `pap`?
On the search page, what does `aria-busy="true"` on the list tell a test?

choices.text: That the list is empty
choices.why: The list can hold an earlier answer and still be busy; at a robot's speed it shows Papaya while busy.

choices.text: That an answer is due
choices.why: Right. The script sets it when a question leaves and clears it when none is outstanding.

choices.text: That the server is overloaded
choices.why: The page cannot see the server's load; it only knows its own requests have not been answered.

choices.text: That the page shows the right result
choices.why: It says nothing about right or wrong, only about whether more answers are coming.

prompt: `papaya` is typed with no pause between keys. Put these answers in the order they reach the page.
trap: The order of the questions is the opposite: the server holds a short question back longer.

prompt: After `papaya` is typed at a robot's speed, the list settles on three fruit. Why those three?

choices.text: They are the fruit whose names contain `p`, the last answer to arrive
choices.why: Right. The answer to `p` is held back longest, lands last and replaces the list.

choices.text: The server ignores every letter after the first one it receives in a query
choices.why: The answer to `papaya` held only Papaya; the server searched the whole word.

choices.text: The page adds every answer to the list
choices.why: `replaceChildren` replaces the list each time; nothing accumulates.

choices.text: They are the first answers to arrive
choices.why: The first to arrive is the answer to `papaya`, with one fruit in it.

prompt: Somebody types `papaya` with 300 ms between keys. Using the server's rule, what does the list end on?

choices.text: Three fruit, as with no pause
choices.why: Above 150 ms a key, each answer lands after the one before it, so the last answer is the one to `papaya`.

choices.text: Two fruit, from the answer to `pa`
choices.why: `pa` leaves 300 ms after `p` and waits 150 ms less, so it is answered later than `p` and earlier than the rest.

choices.text: Papaya alone, the right answer
choices.why: Right. Each question leaves 300 ms after the last and is held only 150 ms less, so the answers land in order.

choices.text: Nothing, because the requests time out
choices.why: No request waits more than 750 ms, and nothing in the page gives up on one.

prompt: Why does the test that uses `fill` pass on a page that shows three fruit to a fast typist?

choices.text: `fill` waits for the network to go quiet
choices.why: `fill` does not wait for the network; the test passes because there was only one request.

choices.text: `fill` cancels the earlier requests
choices.why: There are no earlier requests to cancel: `fill` changes the value once.

choices.text: One change, so one request
choices.why: Right. One `input` event, one answer, and the defect never gets a chance.

choices.text: `fill` types slower than a person
choices.why: It does not type key by key at all; that is `pressSequentially`.

prompt: The test that sleeps 500 ms passed. What does that pass tell you about the page?

choices.text: That the search is correct
choices.why: The page went on to show three fruit; the test looked before that and stopped.

choices.text: Only that at 500 ms the list held one fruit
choices.why: Right. A sleep measures a moment, and this moment fell before the late answers.

choices.text: That the server answered every request
choices.why: At 500 ms the answers to `pa` and `p` had not arrived yet.

choices.text: That 500 ms is the right length for this page
choices.why: No length is right: one second gave the opposite verdict on the same page.

prompt: Which of these tests of the search page give a verdict that depends on timing rather than on the page? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Type key by key, read `count()` at once
choices.why: Right. It reads before any answer, so it fails whatever the page would have shown.

choices.text: Type key by key, sleep 500 ms, read `count()`
choices.why: Right. Its verdict is decided by where 500 ms falls among the answers.

choices.text: Type key by key, wait for `aria-busy="false"`, then check the list
choices.why: It waits for the page to say it is finished, so it reads the final state at any speed.

choices.text: Type key by key, sleep a second, read `count()`
choices.why: Right. It failed on this machine, and on a slower server it could land before the last answer and pass.

prompt: Match each way of waiting to what it waits for.

pairs.right: A length of time, whatever the page does
The list holding one item, at any moment
The page saying no answer is outstanding

prompt: What is the difference between `expect(await list.count()).toBe(1)` and `await expect(list).toHaveCount(1)`?

choices.text: None at all; the second is only a shorter way to write the first
choices.why: The first counts once; the second asks again and again until it is true or time runs out.

choices.text: The first retries until it is true and the second counts once
choices.why: It is the other way round: `toHaveCount` on a locator is the web-first one.

choices.text: The second retries until the count is 1 or time runs out
choices.why: Right. A web-first assertion keeps asking the page, so a slow answer does not fail it.

choices.text: The second also waits for the network to go idle
choices.why: It watches the locator, not the network; on this page it passed while four answers were still coming.

prompt: A test waits for `aria-busy="false"` BEFORE typing, then types and checks the list at once. On the search page, what happens?

choices.text: It works, since the wait is the right condition
choices.why: The condition is right only if it is false until the page is finished, and before typing it is already true.

choices.text: The wait passes at once and the check reads the list too early
choices.why: Right. The HTML starts with `aria-busy="false"`, so the wait is met before anything is asked.

choices.text: The wait never ends, because the attribute starts as `true`
choices.why: On the search page it starts as `false`; the home page's list is the one that starts as `true`.

choices.text: Playwright refuses to let a test wait for anything before an action
choices.why: Nothing stops it; that is why choosing the condition is the author's job.

prompt: A test is marked with `test.fail()` and the defect it describes gets fixed. What does Playwright report the next run?

choices.text: A pass, the same as on every run before the fix
choices.why: It reported a pass while the test failed; now the test passes, which is the opposite of what was declared.

choices.text: A failure: expected to fail, but passed
choices.why: Right. The annotation is now wrong, and deleting it is the fix.

choices.text: A skipped test
choices.why: That is `test.skip()`, which does not run the test at all.

choices.text: Nothing, since tests carrying an annotation are not run
choices.why: `test.fail()` runs the test every time, which is the reason to prefer it here.

prompt: Why is the search test's failure a defect in the shop rather than a flaky test?

choices.text: Because it fails on every run, the same way, for a reason in the page
choices.why: Right. Flaky means sometimes, for a reason outside what is being tested; this is always, and the page is wrong.

choices.text: Because it uses `pressSequentially`
choices.why: The method is how the test reaches the defect, not what makes it one.

choices.text: Because a person typing slowly cannot see it
choices.why: That explains why it was missed by hand, not why it is the page's fault.

choices.text: Because it takes more than five seconds
choices.why: The time comes from the assertion retrying before it gives up; it is not the reason.

prompt: The search page stops loading altogether. What does the test marked with `test.fail()` report?

choices.text: A failure, because the page is broken
choices.why: It fails, as declared, so it is counted as a pass: the annotation accepts any failure.

choices.text: A pass: it failed, as declared
choices.why: Right. That is the weakness of the annotation: it cannot tell the known defect from a new one.

choices.text: A skipped test
choices.why: Nothing skips it; it runs and fails at its first step.

choices.text: An error that names the annotation as wrong
choices.why: Playwright only objects to the annotation when the test passes.

prompt: A filter page reloads a table each time a checkbox is ticked, and sets `aria-busy` on the table while it waits. A test ticks three boxes quickly. What should it wait for before checking the rows?

choices.text: The response to the third request
choices.why: The first two answers may still arrive after it and replace the table, as `p` did.

choices.text: Two seconds, to be safe
choices.why: A guess at the speed of the server; it fails the day the server is slower than the guess.

choices.text: The table's `aria-busy` going back to `false`
choices.why: Right. It is false only when no answer is outstanding, so the rows are final.

choices.text: The table to have at least one row
choices.why: A row from an early answer satisfies it, and the table can still change.

prompt: The Playwright method that types one key at a time, so the page sees one `input` event per key, is ___ .
A developer answers your report with "works for me". Which piece of evidence answers that best?

choices.text: A screenshot of the list with three fruit
choices.why: It shows the result but not how to reach it; the developer will type slowly and see Papaya.

choices.text: The output of `race.mjs` and the failing test
choices.why: Right. Both reproduce it at a robot's speed every time, and the log shows the answers arriving in reverse.

choices.text: A note asking them to type faster
choices.why: It points the right way and proves nothing; a person cannot type at a robot's speed on demand.

choices.text: A second run of the `fill` test
choices.why: That test passes: one request, no race, nothing to show.
